The model's internal correctness direction occupies a language-agnostic low-dimensional subspace that persists even as global representations specialize by language (CKA declines with depth). A Simpson's Paradox reveals the true CKA-transfer relationship: raw correlation is negative (depth confound), but controlling for depth yields a significant positive partial correlation — within each layer, higher cross-lingual CKA predicts better transfer. This local tradeoff shape is architecture-dependent (strong on Qwen, weak on Llama), and combines with the geometric CKA insight to provide a structural explanation for when and why cross-lingual probe transfer succeeds or fails. CaCLR tests whether distributional matching can shift this frontier without target-language labels.

Cross-lingual correctness probes show that deeper layers generally improve both English quality and cross-lingual transfer (Spearman ρ>0.7, p<0.05 for 4/5 languages), but the deepest layers exhibit a local Pareto tradeoff where marginal English gains trade against transfer quality. ### Claim 2 — Decomposition (Analysis)
Cross-lingual correctness transfer decomposes into a difficulty-shared component (language-agnostic, transferable at all depths) and a capability-specific component (language-dependent, driving deep-layer transfer degradation). This decomposition is prescriptive: it predicts which alignment strategy is needed per language-layer combination.
- Evidence: IRT difficulty probes → project out → retrain → compare transfer.

CaCLR (L_BCE + α·L_SB-ECE + β·L_consistency, where L_consistency uses MMD on probe logits computed from parallel inputs — English and target language versions of the same GlobalMMLU train-split items) tests whether joint calibration + cross-lingual invariance optimization can shift the Pareto frontier without target-language correctness labels. - **If consistency loss is inert**: The negative result itself is the contribution — demonstrating that MMD-based distributional matching fails for correctness probe transfer (scope to MMD specifically; acknowledge domain adaptation theory predicts marginal matching failure when conditional distributions differ, cite Zhao et al. 2019).
